## Week 5: functional structures

The methods, introduced together and compared on one task, each a different functional structure for the predictor. Ridge and lasso: what a penalty changes and what $\lambda$ controls. Additive models: a spline as regression on basis functions, one curve per input, the basis size as the knob. Trees: how a small tree predicts and why it is unstable; a random forest as many trees combined into one model. A neural network as a composition, a GLM whose inputs are the outputs of other GLMs, named and fitted and otherwise left for later. Then one simulated dataset for each kind of truth (sparse linear, additive smooth, a step in two inputs at once), every family fitted to each, and the four dimensions on which a method bets: wide or tall, sparse or dense, smooth or discontinuous, additive or interactive. Training error underestimates the risk of a fitted model (the optimism theorem, stated; its proof is yours before the seminar). The three-way split, training, selection and a test set opened once, is used from the first slide. Data: Spotify tracks, what makes a song popular.

**Reading**

- ISLR Chapter 6 (Linear Model Selection and Regularization), sections 6.2.1–6.2.2, pp. 237–250: ridge regression and the lasso, and what each penalty does to the coefficients. Stop before 6.2.3; choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation is week 7.
- ISLR Chapter 7 (Moving Beyond Linearity), sections 7.3–7.4, pp. 294–301 (basis functions and regression splines), and section 7.7, pp. 306–310 (generalized additive models; 7.7.1 fits one by least squares on spline basis functions, as the lecture does, and the GAM part of the lab in 7.8 has the `lm` and `ns()` code). Section 7.5, smoothing splines, is week 7. Skim 7.6, pp. 304–306: local regression, not examined.
- ISLR Chapter 8 (Tree-Based Methods), section 8.1.1, pp. 328–335 (regression trees), and sections 8.2.1–8.2.2, pp. 340–345 (bagging and random forests). Skim 8.1.2–8.1.4, pp. 335–340. Section 8.2.3, boosting, is week 8.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), "Generalization gap", pp. 100–101, the setting of the optimism theorem.
